title: “There Was Someone Crying—There Was!”
paragraphs: Rain hammered down in torrents again the next day. When Mary looked out her window, gray mist and cloud had swallowed nearly all of the moor. Nobody would be going outdoors today.
“What do you all do in your cottage when it rains like this?” she asked Martha.

“Mostly we try not to trip over each other,” Martha answered. “Eh! There do seem a lot of us then. Mother’s a good-tempered woman, but she gets fair worn out and muddled. The biggest ones go out to the cow-shed and play there. Dickon doesn’t mind the wet. He goes out just the same as if the sun was shining. He says he sees things on rainy days that don’t show when it’s fair weather. One time he found a little fox cub half drowned in its hole, and he carried it home inside his shirt to keep it warm. Its mother had been killed close by, and the hole was washed out, and the rest of the litter was dead. He’s got it at home now. Another time he found a half-drowned young crow and brought that home, too, and tamed it. It’s called Soot because it’s so black, and it hops and flies about with him everywhere.”

By now Mary had stopped minding Martha’s friendly way of talking. She had even started to find it interesting, and she was sorry when Martha stopped or went away. The stories her Ayah had told her in India were nothing like Martha’s tales of the moorland cottage, where fourteen people lived in four little rooms and never quite had enough to eat. The children seemed to tumble about and amuse themselves like a litter of rough, good-natured collie puppies. Mary was most drawn to the mother and to Dickon. Whenever Martha told stories about what “mother” said or did, they always sounded comfortable.
“I could play with a raven or a fox cub, if I had one,” said Mary. “But I don’t have anything.”
Martha looked puzzled.
“Can you knit?” she asked.
“No,” answered Mary.
“Can you sew?”
“No.”
“Can you read?”
“Yes.”
“Then why don’t you read something, or learn a bit of spelling? You’re old enough to be learning from your books now.”
“I haven’t any books,” said Mary. “The ones I had were left in India.”
“What a shame,” said Martha. “If Mrs. Medlock would let you into the library, you’d find thousands of books in there.”

Mary did not ask where the library was. A new idea had struck her, and she decided to hunt for the place herself. Mrs. Medlock was no worry, since she seemed to stay in her cozy housekeeper’s sitting-room downstairs. In this odd house you almost never met anyone. Really, there were only the servants to meet, and while the master was away they lived in luxury down below. Their huge kitchen was hung with gleaming brass and pewter, and in their big servants’ hall they ate four or five hearty meals a day. Plenty of noisy, cheerful romping went on there whenever Mrs. Medlock was out of sight.

Mary’s meals were brought to her on time, and Martha waited on her, but no one bothered about her in the least. Mrs. Medlock looked in on her every day or two, but nobody asked what she did or told her what to do. She supposed this was just the English way of treating children. In India her Ayah had always looked after her, following her around and waiting on her hand and foot. Mary had often been tired of having her there. Now nobody followed her. She was learning to dress herself, because Martha looked as if she thought Mary was silly and stupid whenever she wanted things handed to her and put on for her.

“Haven’t you any common sense?” Martha said one day, after Mary had stood waiting for Martha to pull her gloves on for her. “Our Susan Ann is only four years old, and she’s twice as sharp as you. Some days you look fair soft in the head.”
Mary kept her sulky scowl for a whole hour afterward. Still, Martha’s words set her thinking, and she thought several things she had never thought before.

After Martha swept the hearth one last time and went downstairs, Mary stood at the window for some ten minutes this morning. The idea that came to her at the mention of the library was still on her mind. The library itself hardly interested her, since she had read very few books. But the word reminded her of the hundred rooms with their closed doors. Were they all truly locked? What might she find inside if she managed to get into one? Were there really a hundred? She could go and count how many doors she could find. That would give her something to do on a day when she could not go out. Nobody had ever taught her to ask leave before doing things, and she knew nothing whatever about authority. So even if she had met Mrs. Medlock, it would not have crossed her mind to ask whether she might walk around the house.

She opened her door, stepped into the corridor, and began to wander. The corridor was long, and it split into other corridors, and short flights of stairs took her up to yet more of them. Doors lined the way, one after another, and pictures hung on the walls. Some showed dark, curious landscapes, but mostly they were portraits of men and women dressed in strange, splendid costumes of satin and velvet. Soon she was standing in a long gallery with portraits covering every wall. She had never dreamed that a house could hold so many. She walked slowly along it, looking at the faces, and the faces seemed to look back. It felt as though they were asking what a little girl from India was doing in their house. Some portraits were of children. There were little girls in stiff satin frocks that reached their feet and spread out around them, and boys with puffed sleeves, lace collars and long hair, or with large ruffs about their necks. She always paused for the children. She wondered what they had been called, where they had gone, and why they dressed so oddly. One of them was a plain, stiff little girl who looked rather like Mary. She wore a green brocade dress and had a green parrot perched on her finger. Her eyes were sharp and curious.
“Where do you live now?” said Mary aloud to her. “I wish you were here.”

No other little girl can ever have had such a strange morning. The whole huge, rambling house seemed to hold nobody but Mary herself. She roamed up and down, along narrow passages and wide ones, and felt that she was the only person who had ever set foot there. All those rooms had been built, so people must once have lived in them. But everything looked so empty that she could scarcely believe it.

She did not think of turning the handle of a door until she climbed to the second floor. All the doors were shut, just as Mrs. Medlock had said they were. But at last Mary put her hand on the handle of one of them and turned it. For a moment she was almost frightened, because it turned easily, and when she pushed on the door itself, it opened slowly and heavily. It was a massive door, and it opened into a big bedroom. Embroidered hangings covered the wall, and inlaid furniture like the kind she had seen in India stood about the room. A broad window with leaded panes looked out over the moor. Above the mantel was another portrait of the stiff, plain little girl, who seemed to stare at her more curiously than ever.
“Maybe she slept in here once,” said Mary. “The way she stares at me gives me a strange feeling.”

After that she opened door after door. She saw so many rooms that she grew weary, and she began to believe there really were a hundred, though she had not counted. Every one of them held old pictures or old tapestries with odd scenes stitched into them. Almost all had curious furniture and curious ornaments as well.

One room looked like a lady’s sitting-room. Its hangings were all of embroidered velvet, and inside a cabinet stood roughly a hundred small ivory elephants. They came in many sizes. A few carried mahouts or palanquins on their backs. Some were far bigger than the rest, and some were so tiny they looked like babies. Mary had seen carved ivory in India, and elephants were nothing new to her. She opened the cabinet, climbed onto a footstool, and played with them for a good long while. When she grew tired, she lined the elephants up neatly again and closed the cabinet.

All through her wandering in the long corridors and empty rooms she had met nothing alive. In this room, though, she did. As soon as she had shut the cabinet, she heard a tiny rustle. She jumped and turned toward the sofa by the fireplace, where the noise seemed to come from. A cushion lay in the corner of the sofa, and the velvet cover had a hole in it. A small head with a pair of scared eyes was peeping out of the hole.

Mary tiptoed across the room to see. The bright eyes belonged to a little gray mouse. She had gnawed her way into the cushion and built a cozy nest inside. Six baby mice lay curled up asleep beside her. Maybe nobody else was alive in the hundred rooms, but seven mice there did not look lonely in the least.
“If they weren’t so frightened, I would take them back with me,” said Mary.

She had wandered until she was too tired to go farther, so she started back. Two or three times she took the wrong corridor and had to walk back and forth until she found the right one. At last she came out on her own floor again. Even so, she was a good way from her room, and she was not sure where she was.
“I think I’ve taken the wrong turn again,” she said. She stood still where a short passage seemed to end in a wall hung with tapestry. “Which way do I go? It’s so quiet!”

She was standing there, just after she had said this, when a sound broke the stillness. It was another cry, but not quite like the one she had heard the night before. This one was short, a fretful, childish whine muffled by passing through walls.
“It’s closer than before,” said Mary, and her heart began to beat faster. “And it really _is_ crying.”

Without meaning to, she laid her hand on the tapestry beside her, and then she leaped back, badly startled. The tapestry hung over a door, and the door swung open. Behind it was another stretch of the corridor, and up it came Mrs. Medlock, with her bunch of keys in her hand and a very angry look on her face.
“What are you doing in this part of the house?” she said. She grabbed Mary by the arm and yanked her away. “Didn’t I warn you?”
“I took a wrong turn,” Mary explained. “I couldn’t tell which way to go, and then I heard someone crying.” At that moment she truly hated Mrs. Medlock, and a moment later she hated her still more.
“You heard nothing of the kind,” said the housekeeper. “Get back to your nursery this minute, or I’ll box your ears.”
Then she gripped Mary’s arm and hauled her, half pushing and half pulling, along one passage and down the next, until she shoved her through the door of her own room.

“Now listen,” she said. “You stay where you’re told, or you’ll find yourself locked in. The master had better find you a governess, as he promised he would. You’re the sort of child who needs somebody watching her closely, and I have plenty of other work.”
Mrs. Medlock marched out and slammed the door. Mary went and sat on the hearth-rug, white with rage. She did not cry. She ground her teeth instead.
“There _was_ someone crying—there _was_—there _was!_” she said to herself.

Twice now she had heard it, and one day she would find out what it was. She had learned a great deal this morning. It felt as if she had come back from a long journey. And in any case she had been entertained all through it. She had played with the ivory elephants, and she had met the gray mouse and her babies in their nest in the velvet cushion.
